nameStory: The Squatter Pea Crab gets its name from its lifestyle as an uninvited houseguest - it literally squats inside the shells of clams, mussels, and other shellfish without paying rent! These tiny crabs are about the size of a pea, making the name doubly fitting. They're like the ultimate freeloaders of the marine world, setting up shop in someone else's home.
description: The Squatter Pea Crab is a tiny, soft-bodied crab that spends its entire adult life inside the shells of mollusks like clams and mussels. These diminutive crustaceans are typically pea-sized or smaller, with a rounded, somewhat flattened body. Their shell is usually translucent white to pale pink, often with darker spots or mottled patterns. You'll never see them scuttling on the beach - they live their whole lives as tenants inside other creatures' shells.

idTips.label: Size and shape
idTips.description: Extremely small and round, about the size of a pea or smaller, with a soft, somewhat flattened body that feels delicate to the touch

idTips.label: Location found
idTips.description: Always discovered inside opened clams, mussels, or oysters - never free-living on rocks or sand

idTips.label: Shell appearance
idTips.description: Translucent whitish to pale pink shell with darker mottled spots or patches visible through the semi-transparent surface

idTips.label: Body texture
idTips.description: Soft and squishy feeling compared to hard-shelled crabs, with a smooth, almost jelly-like quality when gently touched

idTips.label: Movement
idTips.description: Moves slowly and deliberately inside the host shell, not the quick scuttling motion of typical crabs

habitat: Found along New England's rocky shores and mudflats where their mollusk hosts live, from the intertidal zone down to deeper waters. Look for them inside blue mussels, soft-shell clams, and oysters when collecting shellfish or exploring tide pools. They're most commonly discovered when people are shucking shellfish for dinner.

seasonality.spring: Active inside host mollusks as waters warm. This is when you're most likely to find them while collecting shellfish during low tides.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when both the crabs and their mollusk hosts are most active. Prime time for accidental discovery during clamming or mussel gathering.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to slow down. Often found in shellfish harvested for fall feasts and holiday meals.
seasonality.winter: Dormant period spent deep inside host shells in deeper, warmer waters. Rarely encountered during this season.

funFact: Female Squatter Pea Crabs can actually change the sex of their clam hosts! They release chemicals that turn male clams into females, essentially creating their own food delivery service since female clams filter more water and nutrients that the crabs can steal.
confusionNotes: Most commonly mistaken for a piece of clam meat or debris when first spotted inside a shellfish. The key difference is movement - pea crabs will slowly crawl around while clam parts stay put. Remember: if it's moving inside your dinner, it's probably a pea crab!
contextualKnowledge: Many people discover pea crabs for the first time while preparing shellfish for dinner and mistake them for parasites or signs of spoiled seafood. In reality, finding a pea crab is often considered a sign of a healthy, fresh shellfish - and in some coastal communities, they're even considered a delicacy to be eaten along with the host.
compareHints: Since this is the only Tumidotheres species in New England, compare it with other pea crab family members by its distinctive mottled coloration and preference for bivalve hosts. Other local pea crabs tend to be more uniformly colored and some prefer different host types like sea urchins or tube worms.
